title: Make your own tool
hook: Give a set of steps one name, then use it as often as you like.

warmup.q: A quiz is `quiz = [{"q": "2+2", "a": "4"}]`. Which line gets the answer "4"?
warmup.explain: Pick the item in the list first with [0], then pick the key in that dictionary with ["a"]. List first, then dictionary.
sum adds the numbers in the list: 10 + 20 + 30 is 60.
% gives the remainder. 5 goes into 17 three times (15), and 2 is left over.

why.heading: The same steps, again and again
why.text: On set you do the same routine at every setup: slate, roll, sound speeds, action. Nobody rewrites the routine each time. The 1st AD just says "slate it". Code has the same problem: the same five lines needed in ten places, and if one changes you must fix all ten. A **function** fixes that. It gives a set of steps one name.

why.heading: def teaches Python a new word
why.text:
Here is a function with one step:

`def cheer():`
`    print("Action!")`

The word `def`, a name you choose, brackets, a colon. The indented line (4 spaces) belongs to the function, just like the lines under an `if` or a loop.

why.heading: Defining is not running
why.text:
Writing the `def` only writes the recipe card. Nothing is cooked yet. To run the steps you **call** the function by its name with brackets:

`cheer()`

Call it three times and it runs three times. If you define it but never call it, nothing shows on screen.

why.heading: Parameters are blanks to fill
why.text:
A function gets more useful when it can change a little each time:

`def hello(name):`
`    print("Hi", name)`

`name` is a **parameter**, a blank. When you call `hello("Sam")`, "Sam" fills the blank (it is called the **argument**). With two blanks, the first value fills the first blank, the second fills the second.

why.heading: A one-line note for humans
why.text:
Under the `def` line you can add a **docstring**: one line in triple quotes saying what the function does.

`"""Show one call line."""`

Python ignores it when running. It is a note for the human who reads the code later, and that human is often you in three months.

watch.intro: One function, called three times with different crew. Tap Run.
watch.code:
def call_line(name, clock):
    """Show one crew call line."""
    print(f"{name}: call at {clock}")

call_line("Camera", "06:00")
call_line("Sound", "06:30")
call_line("Makeup", "05:30")
explain: `def call_line(name, clock):` makes the tool. It has two blanks.
The docstring in triple quotes is only a note. Nothing shows for it.
Each call below fills the blanks with new values, so the same steps give three different lines.
Defining the function printed nothing. Only the three calls made output.
watch.break_it: Now break it: change the last line to `call_line("Makeup")` so one value is missing, and tap Run. The error says `TypeError: call_line() missing 1 required positional argument: 'clock'`. That means: the function has two blanks, you filled one. Put the second value back.

tasks.title: Call it three times
tasks.task:
The function `cheer` is already written. Under the comment, call it three times so the screen shows:

`Action!`
`Action!`
`Action!`
tasks.solution:
def cheer():
    print("Action!")

cheer()
cheer()
cheer()
hints: To call a function, write its name and brackets: cheer()
Write cheer() on its own line, and do that three times.
Type cheer() three times, one per line, with no spaces before them.

tasks.title: Fix the slate
tasks.task:
The function `slate` prints the wrong thing. Fix the line inside it, then call it for scene 4 take 2, and scene 4 take 3. The screen must show:

`Scene 4, Take 2`
`Scene 4, Take 3`
tasks.solution:
def slate(scene, take):
    print(f"Scene {scene}, Take {take}")

slate(4, 2)
slate(4, 3)
hints: Inside the brackets you need both blanks, scene and take. An f-string can hold both.
Try print(f"Scene {scene}, Take {take}") and then call slate(4, 2).
The two calls are slate(4, 2) and slate(4, 3), on separate lines.

tasks.title: Gear list tool
tasks.task:
Write a function `gear_line(item, qty)` with a one-line docstring. It prints a line like `2 x C-stand`. Then loop over the `gear` dictionary and call your function for each item. The screen must show:

`2 x C-stand`
`6 x Sandbag`
`4 x Flag`
hints: Two parts. First the def with two blanks. Then a loop with .items() that calls it.
Inside the function: print(f"{qty} x {item}"). The loop is: for item, qty in gear.items():
Under the for line, indent and write gear_line(item, qty). The docstring is a line of triple quotes right under the def.

tests.expect:
2 x C-stand
6 x Sandbag
4 x Flag

recap: `def name(blanks):` makes a function. Indented lines belong to it.
Defining does not run it. Calling `name()` does.
Parameters are blanks. Arguments are the values you fill them with.
A one-line docstring in triple quotes says what the function does.

words.meaning: A named set of steps you can run again and again.
The word that starts making a function.
Running a function by writing its name and brackets.
A blank in the def line that gets filled when you call.
The actual value you put in the brackets when you call.
A one-line note in triple quotes saying what a function does.
